bib.title: Let Me Speak Freely? A Study on the Impact of Format Restrictions on Performance of Large Language Models

question: Do format-restricting instructions and constrained decoding (JSON, XML, YAML) degrade the quality of LLM answers on reasoning and classification tasks?
hypothesis: Format restrictions degrade reasoning, and stricter constraints degrade it more; a second hypothesis (parsing errors explain the gap) was tested and rejected.
contributions: Observe declines in reasoning under format restrictions, stricter constraints generally worse
Offer insights into why performance degrades and propose simple mitigations
Explore JSON, XML and YAML, and three strategies: constrained decoding, format-restricting instructions, NL-to-Format

method.summary: Zero-shot comparison of four levels of format restriction (JSON-mode constrained decoding, format-restricting instructions in JSON/XML/YAML, NL-to-Format two-step, free natural language) on 3 reasoning and 4 classification tasks across 5 (plus 2 additional) LLMs. Each cell is averaged over 9 prompt variants; answers are extracted by an LLM parser.
method.task: Reasoning (GSM8K, Last Letter, Shuffled Objects) and classification (DDXPlus, MultiFin, Sports Understanding, NI Task 280) under output-format restriction

datasets.name: MultiFin
datasets.source: Jorgensen et al., 2023; 5 categories (task prompts list 6)

other.use: Structured Output API (JSON-schema), Sec 5.4, and App D

other.note: chosen as parser for highest agreement with gpt-4-turbo

inference.samples: 9 prompt combinations per model/task/format (3 task descriptions x 3 format descriptions); mean and std reported; seeds/runs not stated
inference.prompting: Zero-shot; fixed template 'Follow the instruction to complete the task: {task_description} Instruct: {format_description} {few shots} {question}'; reasoning tasks include 'Think step-by-step' and reasoning field before answer field; schema has 2 fields (reasoning, answer)

parameters.conditions: JSON-mode (constrained decoding via provider flag or TGI), FRI (JSON/XML/YAML), NL-to-Format (two-step), NL (free text); Sec 5.1 variant removes schema and only names format; Sec 5.3 variant re-prompts Claude-3-Haiku to reformat parse-failed outputs

other.few_shot: template has a few-shot slot but main experiments are called zero-shot

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.definition: classification tasks (Sports, DDXPlus, Task 280, MultiFin) and Shuffled Objects

metrics.name: Exact Match (EM)
metrics.definition: final answer must exactly string-match the gold answer (GSM8K, Last Letter), after LLM answer extraction

metrics.name: Parsing error rate
metrics.definition: share of responses where the answer could not be parsed

metrics.name: Cohen kappa
metrics.definition: agreement of candidate parser LLMs with gpt-4-turbo parsed answers

eval.protocol: LLM-as-parser: claude-3-haiku extracts the final answer (validated against 300 human-parsed samples with gpt-4-turbo: 97.7%); 9 prompt variants per cell, mean (std) reported; no significance test; dataset sizes not stated.

prompts.text: You are a math tutor who helps students of all levels understand and solve mathematical problems. Read the last question carefully and think step by step before answering, the final answer must be only a number.

Provide your output in the following valid JSON format:
```json
{
"step_by_step_reasoning": ...,
"answer": ...
}
```

Provide your output in the following text format:
Step by step reasoning: ...
Answer: The final answer is ...

evidence.quote: we evaluate our approach by nine prompt combinations: three task descriptions and three JSON, XML, and YAML schemas

results.claim: GPT-3.5-turbo JSON-mode responses put the answer key before the reason key in every case on Last Letter, turning zero-shot CoT into direct answering.
results.metric: share of GPT 3.5 Turbo JSON-mode responses with answer before reason
results.quote: we found that 100% of GPT 3.5 Turbo JSON-mode responses placed the "answer" key before the "rea-son" key
results.note: Quote is hyphenated by line wrap in the PDF text.

results.claim: GPT-3.5-Turbo Last Letter exact match falls from text to JSON.
results.setup: Last Letter, gpt-3.5-turbo, zero-shot, mean over 9 prompts, text vs JSON
results.table: Table 9, row GPT-3.5 Turbo JSON, column Last Letter (text 56.7)

results.claim: Claude 3 Haiku GSM8K collapses under JSON with schema (many parsing errors).
results.setup: GSM8K, claude-3-haiku, mean over 9 prompts, JSON vs text
results.table: Table 9, row Claude 3 Haiku JSON, column GSM8K (text 86.5)
results.note: Table 3 gives 60.07% JSON parsing error for Claude-3-Haiku on GSM8K.

results.claim: LLaMA 3 8B GSM8K drops from text to JSON.
results.table: Table 9, row LLaMA 3 8B JSON, column GSM8K (text 74.7)
results.note: Table 1 prints the same JSON+schema as 48.90 and text as 75.13 (Table 9 says 74.7).

results.claim: Removing the schema from the prompt (just naming the format) raises Claude 3 Haiku JSON GSM8K from 23.44 to 86.99.
results.setup: GSM8K, claude-3-haiku, JSON without vs with schema constraint, 9 prompts
results.table: Table 1, row claude-3-haiku, column JSON (no schema 86.99; + schema constraint 23.44)

results.claim: Adding a schema constraint also raises prompt sensitivity: std for gpt-3.5-turbo JSON goes from 1.1 to 12.0.
results.table: Table 1, row gpt-3.5-turbo, JSON (74.70 (1.1) vs + schema 49.25 (12.0))

results.claim: Gemini 1.5 Flash is nearly unaffected by schema on GSM8K JSON.
results.setup: GSM8K gemini-1.5-flash JSON with schema vs without

results.claim: Parsing errors do not explain the gap: LLaMA 3 8B JSON Last Letter parse error is tiny yet the performance gap is large.
results.quote: the parsing error rate for the Last Letter task in JSON format is only 0.148%, yet there ex-ists a substantial 38.15% performance gap as seen in Table 1
results.note: 38.15 does not occur in Table 1; Table 9 shows 70.1 text vs 28.0 JSON (42.1 gap). Table 3 prints 0.15.

results.claim: Using Claude-3-Haiku to reformat outputs with parsing errors recovers large gains for Claude 3 Haiku and LLaMA 3 8B.
results.metric: EM gain from LLM re-parse, e.g. Claude/LLaMA JSON
results.setup: GSM8K and Last Letter, JSON/YAML/XML, Claude-3-haiku and Llama-3-8B, second reformatting prompt
results.note: Assignment of each delta to a model/format read from figure only; 44.8 appears in extracted figure text.

results.claim: Structured Outputs (JSON-schema, gpt-4o-mini) narrows but does not close the gap to natural language on GSM8K.
results.table: Table 2, row GSM8K, columns NL 94.57 / FRI 87.17 / JSON-Mode 86.95 / JSON-Schema 91.71

results.claim: JSON-schema was slightly better than NL on Last Letter for gpt-4o-mini.
results.table: Table 2, row Last Letter, columns NL 83.11 / JSON-Schema 86.07

results.claim: Gemini 1.5 Flash gets a large DDXPlus boost from JSON (constraining answer space), versus text.
results.setup: DDXPlus, gemini-1.5-flash, JSON vs text, mean over 9 prompts
results.table: Table 10, row Gemini-1.5-Flash JSON, column DDXPlus (text 41.6)

results.claim: A regex parser on 'The final answer is (\d+)' greatly under-counts GSM8K accuracy versus an LLM parser.
results.setup: GSM8K, Gemini-1.5-Flash, regex match vs Claude-3-Haiku parser
results.note: Text says Gemini difference is 43.5 points; 69.3-25.8=43.5. Table 8 caption says Claude-3-Haiku parser, text says LLM parser generally.

results.claim: GPT-4-turbo as answer parser matches human parsing on 300 sampled responses.
results.setup: 100 each from Last Letter, Shuffle Obj, GSM8K
results.quote: These findings demonstrate an average align-ment of 97.7% between GPT-4-turbo and human-parsed answers

results.claim: Claude-3-Haiku has highest Cohen's kappa agreement with gpt-4-turbo among low-cost parser candidates.
results.setup: 1,200 NL responses (200 from each of six datasets), reference gpt-4-turbo
results.table: Figure 7 and Appendix B text: claude-3-haiku highest agreement at 0.86
results.note: Appendix text says 'select 200 samples from six datasets ... total 1,200'.

results.claim: Cost per 1000 entries: GPT-3.5-Turbo text format is the most expensive format.
results.setup: averaged over 6 datasets, gpt-3.5-turbo, text vs json
results.note: Table 6 caption says values are processing times in seconds while the text calls them cost; Table 5 says USD.

limits: Authors: no LLaMA 70B or GPT-4o (cost); only small/cheap models
Authors: evaluation datasets limited in scope
Output schemas are minimal (reasoning + answer fields); complex schemas not tested
Temperature, max tokens, per-dataset sizes and seeds not reported
Results for JSON-mode on reasoning are confounded by key order (answer before reason), not constraint per se
Evaluation uses an LLM parser, whose own errors are only validated on 300 samples
Models are mid-2024 versions; OpenAI Structured Outputs only tested on gpt-4o-mini and narrowed the gap

terms.definition: limits the output of LLMs by enforcing predefined token space during the generation process
direct the LLM to generate responses in standardized formats such as JSON, XML, and YAML, adhering to specified schemas
first instructs the LLM to answer the question in natural language, and then instructs it to convert its response into the target format schema

lineage.work: Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in LLMs (Wei et al.)

lineage.note: format-following benchmark, does not test downstream quality
constrained decoding assumed similar to JSON mode
